title: Pseudish insider bloggers can't replace academics
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Vainker argues that popular teacher-bloggers lack the depth to write seriously about education and that the field is poorer for letting them displace academics. His test case is a widely shared post on school culture and character by Pritesh Raichura, which he reads as a post-hoc rationalisation of the Lemov and KIPP behaviour-habit model rather than a real account of character formation. He traces that model back through KIPP and the 1980s academic press to corporate culture borrowed from Japanese car factories, where managing employees' inner values was a means to extract effort. His substantive objection is that scripting granular behaviours leaves no room for Aristotelian phronesis, and produces compliant strivers rather than good people. The piece is polemical and personal, but it makes a genuine intellectual-history argument about where no-excuses school culture comes from.
points: The author contends that classroom experience does not by itself qualify someone to write deeply on school culture or moral development, and that teacher-bloggers have taken over a role academics should play.
The behaviour-habit model of school culture descends from Lemov, KIPP and the 1980s academic press, which borrowed from corporate culture and Japanese car manufacturing.
Such cultures manage pupils' values and identities as well as behaviour, so complying becomes proof of being a good person.
Drilling granular behaviours leaves no space for phronesis, the practical judgement Aristotle saw as central to character.
Vainker concludes the model produces compliant strivers who do well on measures like Progress 8 but are questionable as character formation.
quotes: Experience in teaching and leading is hugely important, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you can write about education interestingly at length. The academic life, whatever its faults (and I’m aware of all the faults), does have the advantage of providing the time and community to explore the big educational questions in sufficient depth. And it is a problem that teacher-bloggers have taken over the role of academics.

In his blog, he sets out how his approach to school culture breeds character. It is trite and complacent, setting out, through a fake Aristotle quote, a pseudo-rationale for his approach to school culture in complete ignorance that the true, quite different, rationale for it was set out over forty years ago (see below).

The same basic principle was passed down: if you want to control an employee/student then controlling their behaviour will only get you so far; you also have to get them to ‘want’ to work hard, and so you need to manage their ‘insides’ - their thoughts, values, feelings; in short - you have to shape their identity to the demands of work.

And so on with every aspect of school life: complying makes me a good person; not complying doesn’t just mean I will get in trouble, it makes me a bad person. And anyway I shouldn’t just comply, I should go above and beyond - that makes me a really good person.

Indeed, some of the very worst people I knew at school were Raichura’s model students- they would thank the teachers, clean their tables, do their work well, but were also vain, thin-skinned, humourless and entitled. They did these things because they wanted to put themselves on the level of the adults, above the rest of us. And they were disliked; we saw that they lacked character.

Raichura’s culture is not about making better people, it’s about making compliant strivers. Instilling such an attitude is good from the perspective of P8, and the attitude might well increase their life chances, but it is entirely questionable when it comes to the development of character.

The post is typical of high-profile teacher-leaders who pronounce about how things should be done from deep inside the bubble. Complacent, prickly, incurious beyond CogSci summaries of summaries and Substacks by peers; possessing far less depth than they realise. The field of education won’t advance with them at the helm.
